subject: SPELLMAN (1962)
object: SPELLMAN (1962) reported familial cases of parkinsonism and presented evidence of a dominant trait in a patient's family.

subject: Kondo et al. (1973)
object: Kondo et al. (1973) performed a genetic analysis of Parkinson disease and reported evidence of a multifactorial etiology.

subject: Kissel and Andre (1976)
object: Kissel and Andre (1976) reported monozygotic twin sisters who both developed Parkinson disease and anosmia at age 39 years. The disease was controlled and regressed with L-dopa treatment. The authors noted that 2 families with the same association had been reported previously.

subject: Kissel and Andre (1976)
object: Kissel and Andre (1976) suggested that a genetically determined anomaly of dopamine metabolism was probably responsible for the combination of Parkinson disease and anosmia in their monozygotic twins.

subject: Young et al. (1977)
object: Young et al. (1977) looked at where affected ancestral second-degree relatives fell in the pedigrees of 12 families with Parkinson disease. Affected relatives were on both sides of the family (bilateral) more often than autosomal dominant inheritance would predict. The authors concluded that this pattern suggested a multifactorial cause for most cases of Parkinson disease, but they did not entirely rule out dominant gene inheritance in some families.

subject: Kessler (1978)
object: Kessler (1978) reviewed Parkinson disease from an epidemiologic perspective.

subject: Duvoisin et al. (1981)
object: Duvoisin et al. (1981) found zero concordance for Parkinson disease in the first 12 monozygotic twin pairs examined in an ongoing twin study. They suggested that genetic factors do not play a major role in the etiology of Parkinson disease.

subject: Duvoisin et al. (1981)
object: In their study of 12 monozygotic twin pairs discordant for Parkinson disease, Duvoisin et al. (1981) noted that one unaffected co-twin had essential tremor, another had cerebrovascular disease, and a third was an alcoholic. Probands appeared to smoke less than co-twins (11.9 vs 16.1 pack-years). Premorbid personality differences between probands and co-twins dated back to late adolescence or early adulthood, which the authors suggested pointed to a prodromal onset of the disease as early as late adolescence or early adult life.

subject: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982)
object: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982) studied 32 patients whose Parkinson disease began before age 40 and identified 3 subgroups: postencephalitic, onset and course with predominant tremor, and onset and course with akinesia and rigidity.

subject: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982)
object: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982) found familial cases in 46% of patients with Parkinson disease starting before age 40, compared with 10-15% in general Parkinson populations. Patients with tremor onset often had relatives with essential tremor. Patients with akineto-rigid onset often had other relatives with Parkinson disease.

subject: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982)
object: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982) reported that familial grey hair, hypertension, diabetes, and thyroid disease appeared more often than expected in the families of patients with early-onset Parkinson disease.

subject: Tune et al. (1982)
object: Tune et al. (1982) published a case report of familial manic-depressive illness occurring together with familial Parkinson disease.

subject: Calne and Langston (1983)
object: Calne and Langston (1983) suggested that in most cases of Parkinson disease the cause may be an environmental factor, possibly toxic, superimposed on a background of slow, sustained neuronal loss due to advancing age.

subject: Ward et al. (1983)
object: Ward et al. (1983) studied 43 monozygotic (MZ) and 19 dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs in which the index case had definite Parkinson disease. Only one MZ pair was definitely concordant. When pairs with questionable clinical features were included, 4 of 48 MZ pairs and 1 of 19 DZ pairs were concordant. The frequency of PD in MZ cotwins was similar to that expected in an unrelated control group matched for age and sex. The authors concluded that the major factors in the etiology of PD are nongenetic, although they could not identify a single environmental agent.

subject: Langston et al. (1983)
object: Langston et al. (1983) described 4 persons who developed marked parkinsonism after intravenous use of an illicit drug. Analysis of the substance injected by 2 of the patients showed mainly 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), with trace amounts of the meperidine analog MPPP. Based on the patients' parkinsonian features and pathologic data from a previously reported case, the authors proposed that MPTP selectively damages cells in the substantia nigra.

subject: Barbeau et al. (1985)
object: Barbeau et al. (1985) studied debrisoquine 4-hydroxylation, a hepatic cytochrome P450 detoxification function, in 40 patients with Parkinson disease and 40 normal controls. Significantly more parkinsonian patients than controls had partially or totally defective 4-hydroxylation of debrisoquine. Poor metabolizers tended to have had earlier onset of disease. The authors postulated that Parkinson disease results from environmental factors acting on genetically susceptible individuals against a background of normal aging.

subject: Teräväinen et al. (1986)
object: Teräväinen et al. (1986) carried out a hospital-based survey of the age-specific prevalence of Parkinson disease in 551 patients from Helsinki and Vancouver. They concluded that the disorder may be starting earlier than it did previously, and they discussed what this might mean for the etiology of Parkinson disease.

subject: Calne et al. (1987)
object: Calne et al. (1987) reported 6 families with Parkinson disease in which symptoms tended to begin at about the same calendar time regardless of patient age. Across generations, the mean difference in time of onset was 4.6 years. The mean difference in age at onset between children and parents was 25.2 years. The authors interpreted this pattern as suggesting an environmental rather than a genetic cause.

subject: Calne et al. (1987)
object: Calne et al. (1987) found no correlation between who developed the disease and degree of consanguinity in their families. They concluded that their findings fit the hypothesis that some cases of Parkinson disease result from early, subclinical environmental damage followed by age-related loss of neurons in the central nervous system.

subject: Duvoisin (1987)
object: Duvoisin (1987) reviewed the genetics of Parkinson disease. He noted that closer study of the clinical data showed that reported familial clusters of parkinsonism reflected various other disorders, notably olivopontocerebellar atrophy (OPCA) and other forms of multiple system atrophy. He also noted that case-control studies had not found a prevalence of PD among first-degree relatives of index cases significantly higher than in control groups.

subject: Duvoisin (1987)
object: Duvoisin (1987) noted that the concordance rate for PD in monozygotic twins had been found to be unexpectedly low and not significantly different from the rate in dizygotic twins or from the prevalence among first-degree relatives. He concluded that the best available data did not support a role of heredity in the etiology of PD, although a nonhereditary, possibly congenital genetic defect was not excluded.

subject: Duvoisin (1987)
object: Duvoisin (1987) noted that the idea that heredity plays a role in PD came first from positive family histories and reports of kindreds with parkinsonism. He added that it was strengthened by the first systematic family study of PD, carried out by Mjones about 50 years earlier.

subject: Di Monte (1991)
object: Di Monte (1991) reviewed evidence that impaired mitochondrial function may underlie neuronal death in Parkinson disease. The evidence included the toxicity of the MPTP metabolite MPP+, which probably acts by blocking mitochondrial electron flow at complex I. It also included reports of reduced mitochondrial complex I activity in the brain and other tissues of parkinsonian patients. Because 7 complex I subunit genes are encoded in the mitochondrial genome, the author suggested that abnormal mtDNA might play a role in PD pathogenesis.

subject: Hughes et al. (1992)
object: Hughes et al. (1992) reported the pathologic findings in 100 patients diagnosed prospectively by consultant neurologists as having idiopathic Parkinson disease. Seventy-six had nigral Lewy bodies; the 24 without Lewy bodies had diagnoses including progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, Alzheimer disease, Alzheimer-type pathology, and basal ganglia vascular disease. Retrospective application of recommended diagnostic criteria improved diagnostic accuracy to 82%.

subject: Hughes et al. (1992)
object: Hughes et al. (1992) found that in all 76 patients with clinically diagnosed Parkinson disease who had nigral Lewy bodies, Lewy bodies were also present in the cerebral cortex. The authors suggested that these observations called into question the concept of Parkinson disease as a single distinct morbid entity.

subject: Kurth et al. (1993)
object: Kurth et al. (1993) used PCR and single-stranded conformational polymorphism (SSCP) analysis after HaeIII digestion to find a polymorphism in the MAOB gene. Allele 1 and allele 2 frequencies were 0.45 and 0.55 in 121 controls, compared with 0.62 and 0.38 in 46 patients with Parkinson disease. Allele 1 was associated with a 2.03-fold relative risk for PD (confidence interval, 1.44-2.61; p < 0.02). A MAOA polymorphism tested in the same groups showed no significant difference in allele frequencies. The authors suggested that an inherited MAOB variant may contribute to a genetic predisposition to PD.

subject: MAOB MAO-B allele 1 (HaeIII SSCP polymorphism)
object: MAOB

subject: Lazzarini et al. (1994)
object: Lazzarini et al. (1994) used a family history questionnaire, an interview and examination of secondary cases to study relatives of PD patients seen consecutively over 1 year. Siblings of probands with an affected parent had a significantly higher cumulative risk of PD than siblings of probands without an affected parent, which suggested significant familial aggregation in a subset of randomly ascertained families.

subject: Lazzarini et al. (1994)
object: In an analysis of 80 multicase PD families, each with 2 or more affected individuals, Lazzarini et al. (1994) found age-adjusted segregation ratios approaching 0.5 and similar proportions of affected parents and siblings. These findings, together with the distribution of affected ancestors, were compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance in a subset of PD.

subject: Bordet et al. (1994)
object: Bordet et al. (1994) analyzed CYP2D6 poor-metabolizer mutations by PCR and XbaI RFLP analysis in 105 Caucasian patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease and 15 patients with diffuse Lewy body disease. The rate of genotypically defined poor metabolizers and the frequency of the D6-B mutation did not differ significantly between the IPD and DLBD patients. The authors found no relationship between CYP2D6 impairment and the spread of neuropathologic lesions, but could not exclude a role for neuronal CYP2D6 expression.

subject: CYP2D6 p.D6
object: CYP2D6

subject: Parboosingh et al. (1995)
object: Parboosingh et al. (1995) screened 107 unrelated patients with Parkinson disease, from familial and sporadic populations, for mutations in the genes for copper/zinc superoxide dismutase (SOD1), manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), and catalase (CAT) using single-strand conformation analysis. They found no mutations and concluded that PD is not caused by mutations in these three free radical detoxifying enzyme genes.

subject: Parboosingh et al. (1995)
object: Parboosingh et al. (1995) identified a glycine-to-aspartic acid substitution in exon 9 of the catalase gene in 1 patient with familial PD, who had decreased red blood cell catalase activity. The authors concluded that this variant was most likely a silent mutation and not the genetic cause of PD in this family.

subject: CAT glycine to aspartic acid substitution in exon 9
object: CAT

subject: Trenkwalder et al. (1995)
object: In a door-to-door survey of 982 individuals older than 65 years in 2 rural Bavarian villages in Germany (response rate 82.5%), Trenkwalder et al. (1995) found a prevalence of Parkinson disease of 0.71% (95% CI, 0.19% to 1.23%), with a male predominance (5 men, 2 women). The prevalence corresponded to that reported in other surveys of people older than 65 years.

subject: Trenkwalder et al. (1995)
object: Trenkwalder et al. (1995) found that parkinsonism of other causes in the same elderly German population included drug-induced parkinsonism (4 of 982), vascular parkinsonism (2 of 982), multiple system atrophy (3 of 982), Fahr disease (1 of 982), and an unexpectedly high prevalence of normal-pressure hydrocephalus (4 of 982); 50% of parkinsonism cases were newly diagnosed.

subject: Markopoulou et al. (1995)
object: Markopoulou et al. (1995) reported a Greek-American kindred with levodopa-responsive parkinsonism in which 16 of 98 individuals across 6 generations developed parkinsonism in 3 successive generations. Affected members were examined in both Greece and the United States. The clinical presentation consisted of asymmetric rigidity, resting tremor, bradykinesia, and postural instability, and symptoms responded to levodopa.

subject: Markopoulou et al. (1995)
object: Markopoulou et al. (1995) concluded that parkinsonism in this Greek-American kindred appeared to be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. They argued that this inheritance pattern, together with the development of parkinsonism in successive generations living on two continents, challenged environmental factors as the main cause of the disease in this kindred.

subject: Markopoulou et al. (1995)
object: Markopoulou et al. (1995) reported anticipation in this kindred. Affected members developed symptoms at ages 50 to 71 years in the third generation, 40 to 55 years in the fourth generation, and 31 years in the fifth generation. They noted that this was another example of a neurodegenerative disease with autosomal dominant inheritance and anticipation.

subject: Ho et al. (1995)
object: Ho et al. (1995) found that a single-stranded conformational polymorphism in the monoamine oxidase B (MAOB) gene was an A or G located 36 bases upstream of the intron 13-exon 14 boundary. In an allelic association study, they found no statistically significant association between this single-base polymorphism and Parkinson disease, which differed from the results of a previous study.

subject: MAOB A or G, 36 bases upstream from the intron 13-exon 14 boundary
object: MAOB

subject: Payami et al. (1995)
object: Payami et al. (1995) studied age at onset and family history in 137 probands with idiopathic Parkinson disease. The 21 probands with an affected parent, aunt, or uncle had a significantly earlier age at onset (47.7 +/- 8.8 years) than the 11 probands with only an affected sib (60.3 +/- 12.9 years) and the 105 probands with no affected sib, parent, aunt, or uncle (59.2 +/- 11.4 years) (p = 0.0001).

subject: Payami et al. (1995)
object: Payami et al. (1995) found that age at onset of affected family members differed significantly between generations (p = 0.0001), being on average 17 years earlier in the proband generation than in the parental generation. Because intrafamily variation in calendar year of onset was too great to suggest a common point of environmental exposure, they concluded that the data were most compatible with genetic anticipation, which could suggest involvement of an unstable trinucleotide repeat.

subject: Planté-Bordeneuve et al. (1995)
object: Planté-Bordeneuve et al. (1995) studied 14 families with clinically typical Parkinson disease. Across 110 first-degree and 40 second-degree relatives, 31 individuals were affected (17 females and 14 males). When compared with 31 age-matched patients with sporadic PD, the familial cases showed no statistical difference in the selected clinical parameters. Clinical parameters and disease course varied within and between families, as in sporadic cases.

subject: Planté-Bordeneuve et al. (1995)
object: Planté-Bordeneuve et al. (1995) found that transmission in 14 families with PD was compatible with an autosomal dominant model. The total segregation ratio of 0.25 suggested incomplete penetrance, which rose with age from 0 below age 30 to 0.43 above age 70.

subject: Planté-Bordeneuve et al. (1995)
object: Planté-Bordeneuve et al. (1995) reported that in 8 multigeneration kindreds, age at onset was earlier in children than in their parents (mean difference 26 +/- 4.6 years, p = 0.01). Within a generation, age at onset was similar (mean difference 4.7 +/- 5.7 years). Although they could not exclude ascertainment bias, the authors suggested that these results were compatible with anticipation.

subject: Bonifati et al. (1995)
object: Bonifati et al. (1995) took family histories in 100 consecutive PD cases, with spouses as controls. Family history of PD was positive in 24% of cases and 6% of spouse controls (p < 0.001). When isolated tremor in relatives was also counted, 43% of cases and 9% of controls had a positive family history (p < 0.001).

subject: Bonifati et al. (1995)
object: Bonifati et al. (1995) found that 9 of the consecutive cases had at least one living affected relative, giving 20 familial PD cases. Compared with sporadic cases from the same consecutive series, the familial cases had an earlier age at onset. The authors concluded that familial and sporadic PD differed only in onset age.

subject: Bonifati et al. (1995)
object: Bonifati et al. (1995) carried out a clinical genetic analysis of 22 non-consecutive PD families, each with at least 2 living, personally examined PD cases (52 PD cases in total). Crude segregation ratios were similar for parents and siblings. Lifetime cumulative risk approached 0.4 in siblings and tended to be comparable in parents, but at later ages. Ancestral relatives were all unilaterally distributed, and the authors concluded that autosomal dominant inheritance with strongly age-related penetrance was most likely.

subject: Bonifati et al. (1995)
object: Bonifati et al. (1995) observed anticipation of age at onset in newer generations of some familial PD families.

subject: Sommer and Rocca (1996)
object: Sommer and Rocca (1996) discussed prion analogues and twin studies in relation to Parkinson disease.

subject: Sandy et al. (1996)
object: In a case-control study comparing CYP2D6 genotypes in 108 patients with young-onset (age 51 years or younger) Parkinson disease and 236 controls, Sandy et al. (1996) found no significant differences in CYP2D6 allele frequencies. The B allele frequency was slightly lower in cases than controls (0.14 vs 0.20; p = 0.10), and neither carriage of one or more B alleles (odds ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.33-1.00) nor carriage of one or more nonfunctional alleles (A, B, D, D2) (odds ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.41-1.13) was associated with increased risk.

subject: CYP2D6 CYP2D6 B allele
object: CYP2D6

subject: Sandy et al. (1996)
object: Sandy et al. (1996) noted that, in contrast with genotyping studies in older-onset PD reporting modest increased risk with CYP2D6 B and A alleles, CYP2D6 alleles were not associated with young-onset PD, and suggested that the young-onset PD population may differ from the older-onset population with respect to risk factors.

subject: Bandmann et al. (1996)
object: Weaver mice show progressive postnatal loss of dopaminergic cells in the mesencephalon and have been proposed as a model for Parkinson disease. Bandmann et al. (1996) therefore sequenced the H5 pore region of hiGIRK2 (KCNJ7), the human homologue of the weaver mouse gene mGIRK2, in familial and sporadic cases of Parkinson disease. The sequence was normal in every case they examined. The authors suggested that nigral cell loss in Parkinson disease and in weaver mice have different causes.

subject: Polymeropoulos et al. (1996)
object: Polymeropoulos et al. (1996) found that genetic markers on chromosome 4q21-q23 were linked to the PD phenotype in a large kindred with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease, with a maximum lod score (Zmax) of 6.00 for marker D4S2380.

subject: Polymeropoulos et al. (1996)
object: Polymeropoulos et al. (1996) noted that Parkinson disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer disease, affecting approximately 1% of the population over age 50, and that studies have confirmed significant familial aggregation of PD, with many large multicase families documented.

subject: Neudorfer et al. (1996)
object: Neudorfer et al. (1996) described 6 patients with type I Gaucher disease, previously considered non-neuronopathic, who developed parkinsonian symptoms, and reviewed the literature. The atypical parkinsonian syndrome was characterized by a relatively severe clinical course with early appearance of neurologic signs in the fourth to sixth decade of life, aggressive progression, and refractoriness to conventional anti-Parkinson therapy.

subject: Polymeropoulos et al. (1997)
object: Polymeropoulos et al. (1997) identified a mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene in a large Italian kindred with Parkinson disease, in which a susceptibility locus had been mapped to chromosome 4q, and in 3 unrelated families of Greek origin with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease. Alpha-synuclein encodes a presynaptic protein thought to be involved in neuronal plasticity.

subject: Polymeropoulos et al. (1997)
object: Polymeropoulos et al. (1997) noted that a Parkinson disease susceptibility gene in a large Italian kindred had recently been mapped to the long arm of chromosome 4.

subject: Polymeropoulos et al. (1997)
object: Polymeropoulos et al. (1997) described Parkinson disease as a common neurodegenerative disorder with a lifetime incidence of approximately 2%, for which familial aggregation has been documented.

subject: Nussbaum and Polymeropoulos (1997)
object: Nussbaum and Polymeropoulos (1997) reviewed how PD research had long focused on environmental factors such as viral infection or neurotoxins. Hereditary influences had been discounted because twin studies found a high monozygotic discordance rate, but those studies were later shown to be inadequate and inconclusive. Interest in hereditary factors returned once a positive family history was recognized as a major risk factor.

subject: Nussbaum and Polymeropoulos (1997)
object: Nussbaum and Polymeropoulos (1997) noted that the common, idiopathic form of PD has a pathological correlate: Lewy bodies, which are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions distributed diffusely throughout the substantia nigra, hypothalamus, hippocampus, autonomic ganglia and olfactory tracts.

subject: Nussbaum and Polymeropoulos (1997)
object: Nussbaum and Polymeropoulos (1997) reviewed the mapping of PD to 4q21-23 by genome-wide scan in one large family with PD and diffuse Lewy bodies, and the finding of a missense mutation in the alpha-synuclein gene in 4 independent PD families. They suggested that at least some familial PD with diffuse Lewy bodies results from an abnormal protein that interferes with normal protein degradation, leading to inclusions and ultimately neuronal cell death. They also proposed that PD alpha-synuclein mutations and Alzheimer disease beta-amyloid and presenilin mutations may share pathogenetic mechanisms.

subject: Scott et al. (1997)
object: Scott et al. (1997) commented on the genetic complexity of Parkinson disease.

subject: Gasser et al. (1997)
object: Gasser et al. (1997) wrote about genetic complexity in Parkinson disease.

subject: Zareparsi et al. (1998)
object: Zareparsi et al. (1998) performed complex segregation analyses on the kindreds of 136 Parkinson disease patients randomly ascertained from a clinic population. They rejected the hypotheses of a nontransmissible environmental factor, of no major gene or type (sporadic), and of all Mendelian inheritance models (dominant, recessive, additive, decreasing) (P less than 0.001). They concluded that familial clustering of PD in this data set was best explained by a rare familial factor that is transmitted in a non-Mendelian fashion and influences the age at onset of PD.

subject: Montgomery et al. (1999)
object: Montgomery et al. (1999) applied a PD test battery, including tests of motor function, olfaction, and mood, to 80 asymptomatic first-degree relatives of PD patients and 100 normal control subjects. Of the first-degree relatives, 22.5% scored in the abnormal range, compared with 9% of controls, a statistically significant difference; relatives with abnormal scores differed on all three components of the battery from relatives with normal scores. The authors suggested that the battery may detect the asymptomatic carrier state or risk for PD.

subject: Montgomery et al. (1999)
object: Montgomery et al. (1999) found that among sons and daughters of PD patients whose PD battery scores were abnormal, the affected parent was much more often the father.

subject: Tanner et al. (1999)
object: Tanner et al. (1999) screened 19,842 white male twins in the National Academy of Sciences/National Research Council World War II Veteran Twins Registry for Parkinson disease and identified 193 twins with PD (concordance-adjusted prevalence, 8.67/1000). In 71 monozygotic (MZ) and 90 dizygotic (DZ) pairs with complete diagnoses, pairwise concordance was similar (0.155 MZ vs 0.111 DZ; relative risk, 1.39; 95% CI, 0.63-3.1). The authors concluded that genetic factors do not play a major role in causing typical PD and that no genetic component is evident when the disease begins after age 50 years.

subject: Tanner et al. (1999)
object: Tanner et al. (1999) found that in 16 twin pairs in which at least 1 twin was diagnosed at or before age 50 years, MZ concordance was 1.0 (4 pairs) and DZ concordance was 0.167 (relative risk, 6.0; 95% CI, 1.69-21.26). They suggested that genetic factors appear to be important when the disease begins at or before age 50 years.

subject: Tanner et al. (1999)
object: Tanner et al. (1999) found 193 twins with PD among 19,842 white male twins in the World War II Veteran Twins Registry, a concordance-adjusted prevalence of 8.67 per 1,000.

subject: Clarke et al. (2000)
object: Clarke et al. (2000) found that neuronal death followed exponential kinetics in 12 models of photoreceptor degeneration, in hippocampal neurons undergoing excitotoxic death, in a mouse model of cerebellar degeneration, and in Parkinson and Huntington diseases. Mathematical models in which the risk of cell death stays constant or falls exponentially with age explained these kinetics better than models of cumulative damage. The authors concluded that this argues against the cumulative damage hypothesis and that the time of death of any neuron is random. They proposed a 'one-hit' biochemical model: the mutation puts the neuron into a mutant steady state, and a single random event starts cell death.

subject: Sveinbjörnsdottir et al. (2000)
object: Sveinbjörnsdottir et al. (2000) reviewed medical records and confirmed the diagnosis of Parkinson disease in 772 living and deceased Icelandic patients diagnosed over the previous 50 years. Using a computerized genealogy database covering 610,920 people in Iceland over 11 centuries, they found that patients with Parkinson disease, including a subgroup of 560 patients with late-onset disease (onset after age 50 years), were significantly more related to each other than matched controls, and this relatedness extended beyond the nuclear family.

subject: Sveinbjörnsdottir et al. (2000)
object: Sveinbjörnsdottir et al. (2000) found that the risk ratio for Parkinson disease among relatives of patients with late-onset disease was 6.7 (95% CI 4.3-9.6) for sibs, 3.2 (95% CI 1.2-7.8) for offspring, and 2.7 (95% CI 1.6-3.9) for nephews and nieces. They concluded that late-onset Parkinson disease has a genetic component as well as an environmental component.

subject: Wu et al. (2001)
object: In a case-control study of 224 Taiwanese patients with Parkinson disease and 197 controls matched for age, sex, and birthplace, Wu et al. (2001) found that the MAOB intron 13 G genotype (G in men and G/G in women) was associated with a 2.07-fold increased relative risk of PD. Genotyping was done by PCR-RFLP analysis.

subject: MAOB MAOB intron 13 G allele
object: MAOB

subject: Wu et al. (2001)
object: Wu et al. (2001) found that the COMT Val158Met polymorphism on its own was not correlated with PD risk in Taiwanese. However, the risk was significantly and synergistically increased in patients carrying both the COMT L (low-activity) and MAOB G genotypes. The authors suggested that these two dopamine-metabolizing enzymes interact in the pathogenesis of sporadic PD, but noted that the combined genotypes were relatively rare in their sample, so the finding needs confirmation in a larger sample.

subject: COMT p.V158M
object: COMT

subject: Vaughan et al. (2001)
object: Vaughan et al. (2001) reviewed the genetics of parkinsonism, describing idiopathic Parkinson disease as a common progressive neurodegenerative disorder whose pathologic hallmarks are Lewy bodies and massive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. They suggested that nigral degeneration with Lewy body formation may represent a final common pathway of a multifactorial disease process in which both environmental and genetic factors have a role.

subject: Vaughan et al. (2001)
object: Vaughan et al. (2001) noted that 2 genes (SNCA and parkin) and 2 further gene loci had been implicated in familial PD, despite large families being rare, heritability in the general population being low, and the disorder being genetically heterogeneous. They also noted that mutations in UCHL1 had been described in familial PD, but that the evidence for its role was less clear.

subject: Tayebi et al. (2001)
object: Tayebi et al. (2001) described a woman with mild Gaucher disease and impaired horizontal saccadic eye movements. She developed a tremor at age 42 years, and her gait then deteriorated rapidly. A pallidotomy at age 47 was unsuccessful, and her motor and cognitive decline continued despite enzyme replacement therapy.

subject: Tayebi et al. (2001)
object: In a patient with mild Gaucher disease and parkinsonism, Tayebi et al. (2001) sequenced the glucocerebrosidase gene and found 2 mutations, L444P and D409H. Southern blot analysis showed an extra 17-kb SspI band on the maternal allele. PCR amplification and sequencing showed a duplication that included the glucocerebrosidase pseudogene, the metaxin gene, and a pseudometaxin/metaxin fusion. The authors suggested that gene changes linked to this rearrangement, which arose from a crossover between metaxin and its pseudogene, could contribute to the patient's atypical phenotype.

subject: GBA1 p.L444P
object: GBA1

subject: GBA1 p.D409H
object: GBA1

subject: Scott et al. (2001)
object: Scott et al. (2001) performed a complete genomic screen with 344 markers in 174 families with multiple individuals diagnosed with idiopathic PD, ascertained through probands in 13 clinic populations in the continental United States and Australia; 870 family members were studied (378 affected, 379 unaffected, 113 unclear status). Two-point parametric and multipoint nonparametric linkage analysis detected evidence for linkage to chromosomes 17q (MLOD = 2.28; LOD = 2.62), 8p (MLOD = 2.01; LOD = 2.22), and 5q (MLOD = 2.39; LOD = 1.50) overall and in families with late-onset PD, and to chromosome 9q (MLOD = 1.52; LOD = 2.59) in families with both levodopa-responsive and levodopa-nonresponsive patients.

subject: Scott et al. (2001)
object: In the genomic screen by Scott et al. (2001), significant linkage to the parkin gene region on chromosome 6 (MLOD = 5.07; LOD = 5.47) was found in families with at least 1 individual with PD onset before age 40 years. The authors concluded that parkin is important in early-onset PD and that multiple genetic factors may be important in idiopathic late-onset PD.

subject: Martin et al. (2001)
object: Martin et al. (2001) tested 5 SNPs within the tau gene (MAPT) for association with idiopathic Parkinson disease using family-based association tests in 1,056 individuals (426 affected, 579 unaffected, 51 with unclear status) from 235 families recruited at 13 clinical centers in the United States and Australia and a family ascertainment core center. Three of the 5 SNPs showed significant association (SNP 3, P = 0.03; SNP 9i, P = 0.04; SNP 11, P = 0.04), whereas SNP 9ii and SNP 9iii did not. Haplotype analysis showed strong evidence of association, with one haplotype positively associated (P = 0.009) and another negatively associated (P = 0.007), and substantial linkage disequilibrium (P less than 0.001) was found among SNPs 3, 9i, 9ii, and 11. The authors concluded that tau is a susceptibility gene for idiopathic PD.

subject: Martin et al. (2001)
object: Martin et al. (2001) noted that they had previously observed linkage of idiopathic PD to a region on chromosome 17q21 that contains the tau gene, and concluded that this integrated linkage and positional association approach implicated tau as a susceptibility gene for idiopathic PD.

subject: Auluck et al. (2002)
object: Auluck et al. (2002) found that directed expression of the molecular chaperone Hsp70 prevented the dopaminergic neuronal loss associated with alpha-synuclein expression in Drosophila, and that interfering with endogenous chaperone activity accelerated alpha-synuclein toxicity.

subject: Auluck et al. (2002)
object: Auluck et al. (2002) found that Lewy bodies in human postmortem brain tissue immunostained for molecular chaperones. They suggested that chaperones may play a role in the progression of Parkinson disease.

subject: Racette et al. (2002)
object: Racette et al. (2002) described a large, multi-incident Old-Order Amish pedigree with PD. Of 113 examined members, 17 had clinically definite, 6 clinically probable and 23 clinically possible PD. Mean age at onset in the clinically definite subjects was 56.7 years. The phenotype was typical of idiopathic PD: rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability and response to levodopa. Dementia occurred in 6 of the clinically definite subjects, and many had levodopa-related motor complications, including wearing off and dyskinesias.

subject: Racette et al. (2002)
object: Racette et al. (2002) found that the mean kinship coefficient in Amish subjects with PD or with PD by history (0.036) was significantly higher (p = 0.007) than in age-matched normal Amish controls (0.016). The authors took this as evidence that PD is inherited in this family.

subject: Racette et al. (2002)
object: Racette et al. (2002) calculated a minimum PD prevalence of 552 per 100,000 among people aged 40 years and older in the index Old-Order Amish community. They concluded that PD is more common in this community than in the general population.

subject: Racette et al. (2002)
object: In the Amish kindred, Racette et al. (2002) sequenced genes with known PD-causing mutations and found no mutations. No single haplotype cosegregated with the disease in any chromosomal region previously linked to PD, and no marker in these regions showed increased homozygosity among definite cases. The authors suggested that the increased prevalence may be due in part to a novel gene or genes.

subject: Li et al. (2002)
object: Li et al. (2002) performed a genomic screen for age at onset (AAO) in 174 families with Parkinson disease and 449 families with Alzheimer disease. Heritability of AAO was 40 to 60% in both data sets. For PD, they found significant evidence for linkage of AAO to chromosome 1p (lod = 3.41).

subject: Li et al. (2002)
object: Li et al. (2002) identified evidence for AAO linkage on chromosomes 6 and 10 independently in both the AD and PD data sets; unified analysis identified a single peak on chromosome 10q between D10S1239 and D10S1237 (maximum lod score 2.62). The authors suggested that a common gene affects age at onset in these two neurodegenerative diseases.

subject: Maher et al. (2002)
object: Maher et al. (2002) performed segregation analysis on the nuclear families of 948 consecutively ascertained PD index cases from 3 US centers (University of Virginia, UMDNJ-Robert Wood Johnson, and Boston University). The analyses supported the presence of a rare major Mendelian gene for PD in both age-of-onset and susceptibility models; the age-of-onset model suggested a gene influencing age-dependent penetrance rather than susceptibility, and it was not evident whether the two analyses modeled the same gene or different genes.

subject: Maher et al. (2002)
object: In the 948 PD index cases studied by Maher et al. (2002), 60.4% were male and 39.6% female, with a mean age of onset of 57.7 years; affected relatives included fathers (4.7%), mothers (6.6%), brothers (2.9%), and sisters (3.2%), proportions similar across the 3 sites. While most index cases were male, modestly more reported affected relatives were female.

subject: Maher et al. (2002)
object: Maher et al. (2002) suggested that the significant genes influencing PD penetrance may interact with environmental factors or other genes, and that such gene-environment interactions involving reduced penetrance may explain the low concordance rates among monozygotic twins for PD.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2002)
object: Pankratz et al. (2002) studied 203 PD sib pairs who had a rigorous neurologic assessment. They excluded 22 families with parkin mutations and ran a genome screen with multipoint nonparametric linkage analysis in 160 multiplex families. With verified PD only (model I; 96 sib pairs from 90 families), the highest lod scores were on chromosome X (2.1) and chromosome 2 (1.9). With all examined individuals counted as affected (model II; 170 sib pairs from 160 families), the lod scores rose to 2.7 for chromosome X and 2.5 for chromosome 2.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2002)
object: Pankratz et al. (2002) also found evidence of linkage to chromosomes 4, 5, and 13, with lod scores above 1.5. They noted that these results agreed with other linkage studies that had reported linkage to chromosomes 5 and X.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2002)
object: Pankratz et al. (2002) identified parkin mutations in 22 of the PD sib-pair families after prioritizing families with positive lod scores for a marker in a parkin intron. They excluded these families from the genome screen to reduce genetic heterogeneity.

subject: Mattila et al. (2002)
object: Mattila et al. (2002) reported an association between a polymorphism at position -511 in the interleukin-1-beta gene (IL1B) and Parkinson disease in Finnish patients.

subject: IL1B -511
object: IL1B

subject: Levecque et al. (2003)
object: In a community-based case-control study of 209 Parkinson disease patients and 488 controls of European (mostly French) ancestry, Levecque et al. (2003) found associations with a polymorphism in exon 22 of iNOS (NOS2) (OR for AA carriers = 0.50, 95% CI 0.29-0.86, P = 0.01) and a polymorphism in exon 29 of nNOS (NOS1) (OR for T allele carriers = 1.53, 95% CI 1.08-2.16, P = 0.02). They found no association with a polymorphism in exon 18 of nNOS (OR for T allele carriers = 1.20, P = 0.30). Subjects were enrolled through the Mutualite Sociale Agricole, the French health insurance organization for agricultural workers, and controls were matched for age, sex and region of residence.

subject: NOS2 polymorphism in exon 22 of iNOS
object: NOS2

subject: NOS1 polymorphism in exon 18 of nNOS (T allele)
object: NOS1

subject: Levecque et al. (2003)
object: Levecque et al. (2003) found a significant interaction between the nNOS polymorphisms and current or past cigarette smoking (nNOS exon 18, P = 0.05; nNOS exon 29, P = 0.04). They concluded that the data favor NOS1 and NOS2 as new modifier genes in PD.

subject: Várkonyi et al. (2003)
object: Várkonyi et al. (2003) reported 4 adult patients with type 1 Gaucher disease who also had parkinsonism. Their parkinsonian signs began relatively early, progressed quickly, and did not respond to therapy.

subject: Várkonyi et al. (2003)
object: Várkonyi et al. (2003) found that each of the 4 patients with both Gaucher disease and parkinsonism had a different Gaucher genotype, and that 4 of the alleles carried the common N370S mutation. No mutations were found in the parkin or alpha-synuclein genes. The authors suggested that the two phenotypes occur together because of a shared pathway, a modifier, or another genetic cause.

subject: GBA1 p.N370S / p.R496M / p.V394L
object: GBA1

subject: van der Walt et al. (2003)
object: van der Walt et al. (2003) genotyped 10 SNPs that define the European mtDNA haplogroups in 609 white patients with PD and 340 unaffected white controls. People in haplogroup J (OR 0.55; 95% CI 0.34-0.91; P = 0.02) or haplogroup K (OR 0.52; 95% CI 0.30-0.90; P = 0.02) had a significantly lower risk of PD than people in the most common haplogroup, H.

subject: van der Walt et al. (2003)
object: van der Walt et al. (2003) found that 10398G, an mtDNA SNP that defines haplogroups J and K, was strongly associated with a lower risk of PD (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.39-0.73; P = 0.0001). This SNP changes threonine to alanine, a nonconservative substitution, in the ND3 subunit of complex I. After stratifying by sex, the protective effect appeared stronger in women (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.27-0.71; P = 0.0009). The authors suggested that ND3 is an important factor in PD susceptibility among white individuals.

subject: MT-ND3 10398G
object: MT-ND3

subject: van der Walt et al. (2003)
object: van der Walt et al. (2003) found that SNP 9055A in the mitochondrial ATP6 gene had a protective effect against PD in women (OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.22-0.93; P = 0.03).

subject: MT-ATP6 9055A
object: MT-ATP6

subject: Chan et al. (2003)
object: Chan et al. (2003) studied 99 Chinese patients with PD and 126 controls from 2 Hong Kong hospitals and used PCR-RFLP to genotype the M1, M2, and M3 slow acetylator polymorphisms of NAT2. The slow acetylator genotype was much more frequent in patients than in controls (68.7% vs 28.6%), with an odds ratio of 5.53 (95% CI 3.08-9.92) after adjusting for age, sex, and smoking history. In a subgroup analysis, smoking did not change the association. The authors suggested that the association was evidence for a possible functional relationship between the NAT2 slow acetylator genotype and PD.

subject: NAT2 M1
object: NAT2

subject: NAT2 M2
object: NAT2

subject: NAT2 M3
object: NAT2

subject: Warner and Schapira (2003)
object: In a review, Warner and Schapira (2003) summarized evidence for a genetic role in Parkinson disease from twin and family studies, from mapping and cloning PARK genes, and from studies of possible susceptibility genes. They also reviewed evidence that environmental factors may play a part. They concluded that most cases probably result from a complex interplay between genetic and environmental influences.

subject: Gill et al. (2003)
object: In a phase 1 safety trial, Gill et al. (2003) delivered glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) directly into the putamen of 5 patients with Parkinson disease. One catheter had to be repositioned, and MRI changes resolved after the GDNF concentration was lowered. After 1 year there were no serious clinical side effects. The off-medication UPDRS motor subscore improved by 39%, and the activities of daily living subscore improved by 61%.

subject: Gill et al. (2003)
object: Gill et al. (2003) reported that during chronic intraputaminal GDNF delivery, medication-induced dyskinesias fell by 64% and did not occur off medication. PET scans of [18F]dopamine uptake showed a significant 28% increase in putamen dopamine storage after 18 months, which the authors suggested reflected a direct effect of GDNF on dopamine function.

subject: Teismann et al. (2003)
object: Teismann et al. (2003) found that COX-2, the rate-limiting enzyme in prostaglandin E2 synthesis, was upregulated in brain dopaminergic neurons of both PD patients and MPTP-treated mice. They concluded that COX-2 has a critical role in both the pathogenesis and selectivity of the PD neurodegenerative process.

subject: Teismann et al. (2003)
object: In MPTP-treated mice, Teismann et al. (2003) showed that COX-2 induction occurred through a JNK/c-Jun-dependent mechanism. Targeting COX-2 protected against MPTP-induced dopaminergic neurodegeneration not by mitigating inflammation but by preventing formation of the oxidant species dopamine-quinone, which has been implicated in PD pathogenesis.

subject: Teismann et al. (2003)
object: Teismann et al. (2003) suggested that COX-2 inhibitors may be therapies for PD, because they have a good safety record and can cross the blood-brain barrier.

subject: Marx et al. (2003)
object: Marx et al. (2003) screened the synphilin-1 gene (SNCAIP) in 328 German patients with familial or sporadic PD and identified a heterozygous C-to-T transition at coding position 1861 resulting in an arg621-to-cys (R621C) substitution in 2 apparently sporadic PD patients. The mutation was absent in 702 control chromosomes from healthy Germans.

subject: SYNPHILIN-1 c.1861C>T / p.R621C
object: SYNPHILIN-1

subject: Marx et al. (2003)
object: In functional studies in SH-SY5Y cells, Marx et al. (2003) found that synphilin-1 produced cytoplasmic inclusions; under proteasomal inhibition, cells expressing C621 synphilin-1 formed significantly fewer inclusions than cells expressing wildtype synphilin-1, and C621-expressing cells were more susceptible to staurosporine-induced cell death. The authors suggested a causative role for R621C in PD and that inclusion formation may be beneficial, with the mutation sensitizing neurons to cellular stress.

subject: Bembi et al. (2003)
object: Bembi et al. (2003) described 4 patients with type 1 Gaucher disease, 2 of whom were sibs, who had typical Parkinson disease. Features included asymmetric onset of rigidity, resting tremor, bradykinesia, and a good response to antiparkinsonian therapy. The authors contrasted this with earlier reports, in which PD with Gaucher disease mainly showed bilateral akinetic-rigid signs and a poor response to levodopa.

subject: Scherzer et al. (2003)
object: Scherzer et al. (2003) profiled expression of the entire Drosophila genome at presymptomatic, early, and advanced disease stages in transgenic flies expressing human alpha-synuclein, which replicate age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons, Lewy body-like inclusions, and locomotor impairment. Fifty-one signature transcripts, including lipid, energy, and membrane transport mRNAs, were tightly associated with alpha-synuclein expression, and expression changes revealed specific pathology already at the presymptomatic stage. In age-matched tau transgenic flies, transcription of the alpha-synuclein-associated genes was normal, suggesting highly distinct pathways of neurodegeneration.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2003)
object: Pankratz et al. (2003) performed genome-wide nonparametric linkage analysis in 754 affected individuals comprising 425 sib pairs from 362 multiplex Parkinson disease families. Under a model restricted to individuals with verified PD (216 sib pairs), the maximum lod score was 3.4 on chromosome 2; under a model including all affected individuals (425 sib pairs), a lod score of 3.1 was obtained on the X chromosome.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2003)
object: In the 85 families of Pankratz et al. (2003) with a very strong family history of PD, a genome screen gave strong evidence of linkage to chromosome 2 (lod = 4.9) and also a lod score of 2.4 on chromosome 14. In the 277 families without a strong family history, linkage was detected to chromosomes 10 (lod = 2.4) and X (lod = 3.2). The authors concluded that there was consistent evidence of linkage to chromosomes 2 and X.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2003)
object: Pankratz et al. (2003) screened the parkin gene in a subset of families with earlier onset or positive lod scores at a parkin marker. A genome screen in the 23 families with PD patients carrying a mutation in only one parkin allele detected evidence of linkage to chromosome 10 (lod = 2.3). The authors concluded that their findings supported the hypothesis that gene-by-gene (epistatic) interactions are important in PD susceptibility.

subject: Marder et al. (2003)
object: Marder et al. (2003) estimated PD risk in first-degree relatives of 221 PD probands with onset at age 50 years or younger and 266 probands with onset after age 50, compared with first-degree relatives of 409 control probands. Risk was similarly increased among first-degree relatives of early-onset probands (risk ratio (RR) 2.9; 95% CI 1.6-5.0) and late-onset probands (RR 2.7; 95% CI 1.6-4.4).

subject: Marder et al. (2003)
object: Marder et al. (2003) found that in late-onset PD families, both siblings (RR 3.6; 95% CI 1.3-10.3) and parents (RR 2.5; 95% CI 1.4-4.6) of probands were at increased risk compared with control relatives, whereas in early-onset families siblings (RR 7.9) but not parents (RR 1.7, not significant) were at increased risk. They concluded this pattern was consistent with an autosomal recessive contribution to early-onset but not late-onset PD, and that genetic factors are important in both, but the specific genes and mode of inheritance may differ.

subject: Li et al. (2003)
object: Li et al. (2003) used 'genomic convergence' to prioritize candidate genes in a 15-cM region on chromosome 10q that they had previously linked to age at onset in Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease. Expression studies of hippocampus from AD patients and controls found 4 genes in the linkage region whose expression differed significantly: stearoyl-CoA desaturase, NDUFB8, PRSS11, and GSTO1.

subject: Li et al. (2003)
object: In allelic association studies of age at onset using 1,362 samples from a PD dataset (635 PD patients) and 2,814 samples from an AD dataset (1,773 AD patients), Li et al. (2003) found no association for 3 of the candidate genes. They did find a significant association for GSTO1 (P = 0.007) and for the neighbouring gene GSTO2 (P = 0.005). They noted that GSTO1 may be involved in the posttranslational modification of interleukin-1-beta, which they called provocative given reports that inflammation may play a role in these disorders.

subject: Tan et al. (2004)
object: Tan et al. (2004) carried out a 3-phase door-to-door community survey of a random sample of 15,000 people aged 50 years and older (9,000 Chinese, 3,000 Malays, 3,000 Indians) in central Singapore, with a 67% participation rate. They identified 46 people with Parkinson disease, 16 of whom had not been diagnosed before. The prevalence of PD in people aged 50 and older was 0.30% (age-adjusted to the 1970 US census) and rose significantly with age. Age-adjusted prevalence was the same in Chinese (0.33%), Malays (0.29%), and Indians (0.28%) (p = 1.0). The authors concluded that prevalence was comparable to that in Western countries and suggested that environmental factors may be more important than racially determined genetic factors in the development of PD.

subject: Wirdefeldt et al. (2004)
object: Wirdefeldt et al. (2004) studied PD in same-sex and opposite-sex twin pairs from the Swedish Twin Registry. They screened 33,780 twins in 14,082 pairs by telephone interview and by linkage to the Swedish Inpatient Discharge Register. They identified 247 twins with possible PD and 517 with suspected parkinsonism or movement disorder. For possible PD there were only 2 concordant pairs, both female and dizygotic. Concordance stayed low in all zygosity groups when the definition of affected was broadened.

subject: Wirdefeldt et al. (2004)
object: Wirdefeldt et al. (2004) found that the best-fitting structural equation model included only environmental components of variance. Results suggested a slightly larger familial component in women. The authors concluded that environmental factors are most important in the etiology of PD and that genetic effects in PD are notably less important than in other complex diseases.

subject: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004)
object: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004) screened 99 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, 74 Ashkenazi patients with Alzheimer disease, and 1,543 healthy Ashkenazi controls for the 6 GBA mutations most common among Ashkenazi Jews (N370S, L444P, 84GG, IVS+1, V394L, and R496H). Thirty-one PD patients (31.3%) had 1 or 2 mutant GBA alleles: 23 were heterozygous for N370S, 4 heterozygous for 84GG, 3 homozygous for N370S, and 1 heterozygous for R496H, compared with 4.1% of Alzheimer patients and 6.2% of controls being Gaucher carriers.

object: GBA1

subject: GBA1 p.R496H
object: GBA1

subject: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004)
object: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004) found that Ashkenazi Jewish patients with Parkinson disease had significantly greater odds of being Gaucher disease (GBA mutation) carriers than patients with Alzheimer disease (odds ratio 10.8; P less than 0.001) or controls (odds ratio 7.0; P less than 0.001), and suggested that heterozygosity for a GBA mutation may predispose Ashkenazi Jews to PD.

subject: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004)
object: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004) found that among Ashkenazi PD patients, GBA mutation carriers had a younger age at onset than noncarriers (mean 60.0 vs 64.2 years; P = 0.04).

subject: Stien (2005)
object: Stien (2005) discussed descriptions of parkinsonism in the works of Shakespeare.

subject: Paleacu et al. (2005)
object: Paleacu et al. (2005) studied 276 outpatients with Parkinson disease and found hallucinations in 32% of them. In a stepwise logistic regression, risk factors for hallucinations were Mini-Mental State Examination score (p < 0.0001) and a positive family history of dementia (p = 0.0005). The authors concluded that a family history of dementia and lower MMSE scores are risk factors for hallucinations in PD.

subject: Maraganore et al. (2005)
object: Maraganore et al. (2005) carried out a two-tiered whole-genome association study of Parkinson disease. In tier 1 they genotyped 198,345 SNPs in 443 sibling pairs discordant for PD. In tier 2a they genotyped 1,793 PD-associated SNPs in 332 matched case-unrelated control pairs. Eleven SNPs were associated with PD (P<.01) in both tiers with the same direction of effect, and the lowest combined P value (P = 7.62 x 10(-6)) was for a SNP within the semaphorin 5A gene (SEMA5A). The authors noted that SEMA5A plays a role in neurogenesis and neuronal apoptosis, which is consistent with existing hypotheses of PD pathogenesis.

subject: Maraganore et al. (2005)
object: In the whole-genome association study by Maraganore et al. (2005), a second SNP among the top associations tagged the PARK11 late-onset PD susceptibility locus (P = 1.70 x 10(-5)).

subject: Maraganore et al. (2005)
object: In tier 2b, Maraganore et al. (2005) genotyped 941 SNPs that were borderline significant in tier 1 (P<.05) and that tested a priori hypotheses about PD susceptibility. In the combined tier 1 and tier 2b data, the 2 SNPs with the lowest P values (P = 9.07 x 10(-6) and P = 2.96 x 10(-5)) tagged the PARK10 late-onset PD susceptibility locus. The authors said that independent replication across populations was needed.

subject: Kwok et al. (2005)
object: Kwok et al. (2005) identified 2 functional SNPs in the GSK3B gene. In vitro, the T allele of the promoter SNP rs334558 had greater transcriptional activity. The intronic SNP rs6438552 regulated the choice of splice acceptor site in vitro, and its T allele was associated with altered splicing in lymphocytes and higher levels of GSK3B transcripts lacking exons 9 and 11 (GSK-delta-exon9+11). Higher levels of this transcript correlated with increased phosphorylation of its substrate, tau.

subject: GSK3B rs334558
object: GSK3B

subject: GSK3B rs6438552
object: GSK3B

subject: Kwok et al. (2005)
object: Kwok et al. (2005) found that the T allele of rs6438552 was more frequent in PD brains than in control brains. PD brains also had correspondingly higher levels of the GSK-delta-exon9+11 transcript and more tau phosphorylation.

subject: Kwok et al. (2005)
object: Using conditional logistic regression, Kwok et al. (2005) found a gene-gene interaction between the T/T genotype of GSK3B rs334558 and the H1/H1 haplotype of MAPT (p = 0.009). After stratifying by tau haplotype, a GSK3B haplotype carrying the T allele at both SNPs was associated with PD risk. The odds ratio was 1.64 in H1/H2 and H2/H2 individuals (p = 0.007) and 0.68 in H1/H1 individuals (p less than 0.001). The authors suggested that GSK3B polymorphisms interact with tau haplotypes to modify PD risk.

subject: Fujita et al. (2006)
object: Fujita et al. (2006) used SPECT with the ligand [123I]5-IA to image nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in 10 nondemented Parkinson disease patients and 15 age-matched healthy controls. Compared with controls, the patients had a widespread, significant decrease of about 10% in total distribution volume in both cortical and subcortical regions, with no significant change in delivery (K1). The authors said the results indicated the importance of extending the study to demented patients.

subject: Toft et al. (2006)
object: Toft et al. (2006) screened 311 Norwegian patients with Parkinson disease and 474 controls for 2 common functional GBA mutations, N370S and L444P. Seven patients (2.3%) and 8 controls (1.7%) carried a mutant GBA allele (p = 0.58). The authors concluded that their study did not indicate increased susceptibility to PD in GBA mutation carriers in Norway.

subject: Botella-López et al. (2006)
object: Botella-López et al. (2006) found that the 180-kDa Reelin band in cerebrospinal fluid was increased in all the neurodegenerative disorders they studied, including Parkinson disease, frontotemporal dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy, and Alzheimer disease. Levels of 180-kDa Reelin correlated positively with CSF Tau protein. The authors suggested that Reelin is involved in the pathogenesis of a number of neurodegenerative diseases.

subject: Muqit et al. (2006)
object: In a review, Muqit et al. (2006) noted that impairment of mitochondrial function is thought to play a major role in the pathogenesis of Parkinson disease, and that recent genetic advances suggest that mitochondrial dysfunction may be the primary defect. They suggested that drugs targeting mitochondria may represent the best hope for disease-modifying therapies.

subject: Zhang et al. (2006)
object: Zhang et al. (2006) reviewed early descriptions of Parkinson disease in ancient China.

subject: Cooper et al. (2006)
object: Cooper et al. (2006) found that in yeast the earliest defect following alpha-synuclein expression was a block in endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking. In a genomewide screen, the largest class of toxicity modifiers were proteins functioning at this same step, including the Rab GTPase Ypt1p, which associated with cytoplasmic alpha-synuclein inclusions.

subject: Cooper et al. (2006)
object: Cooper et al. (2006) showed that elevated expression of Rab1, the mammalian homolog of yeast YPT1, protected against alpha-synuclein-induced dopaminergic neuron loss in animal models of PD. The authors suggested that synucleinopathies may result from disruptions in basic cellular functions that interface with the unique biology of particular neurons to make them especially vulnerable.

subject: Kreitzer and Malenka (2007)
object: Kreitzer and Malenka (2007) found that in striatum, excitatory synapses onto indirect-pathway medium spiny neurons (MSNs) had higher release probability and larger NMDA receptor currents than direct-pathway synapses. Only indirect-pathway MSNs showed endocannabinoid-mediated long-term depression (eCB-LTD), and this LTD needed dopamine D2 receptor activation.

subject: Kreitzer and Malenka (2007)
object: In models of Parkinson disease, Kreitzer and Malenka (2007) found that indirect-pathway eCB-LTD was absent. A D2 receptor agonist or inhibitors of endocannabinoid degradation restored it. Giving these drugs together in vivo reduced parkinsonian motor deficits. The authors suggested that endocannabinoid-mediated depression of indirect-pathway synapses plays a critical role in controlling movement.

subject: Voon et al. (2007)
object: Voon et al. (2007) compared 21 patients with idiopathic PD who developed pathological gambling after starting medication with 42 consecutive PD patients without compulsive behaviors. Patients with pathological gambling had younger age at PD onset, higher novelty seeking, medication-induced hypomania or mania, impaired planning, and a personal or immediate family history of alcohol use disorders. Novelty seeking, alcohol use disorder history, and younger age at onset predicted pathological gambling with 83.7% accuracy in a logistic regression model, and the authors concluded that such patients may have a greater risk for pathological gambling with dopamine agonists.

subject: Constantinescu et al. (2007)
object: Constantinescu et al. (2007) found 5 cases of malignant melanoma in the DATATOP clinical trial cohort of patients with early Parkinson disease. In a standard healthy population, 1.5 cases would be expected. The standardized event ratio was 3.3 (95% CI, 1.1-7.8), which showed a higher-than-expected incidence of melanoma. The authors found no association between levodopa therapy and melanoma incidence.

subject: Ferreira et al. (2007)
object: In a cross-sectional survey, Ferreira et al. (2007) had a movement disorder specialist and a dermatologist examine 150 patients with Parkinson disease and 146 age-matched controls. Neoplastic or preneoplastic skin lesions were present in 35 PD patients (23.3%) and 20 controls (13.7%) (OR 1.92; 95% CI 1.05-3.51). The difference was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for sex, because controls were matched only for age and the PD group had more males. Twenty-nine PD patients (19%) had actinic keratosis and 4 (3%) had basal cell carcinoma. The authors called their results nonconclusive but said they agreed with previous studies suggesting an increased risk of skin cancer in PD.

subject: Chan et al. (2007)
object: Chan et al. (2007) suggested that dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta rely unusually on L-type Cav1.3 calcium channels to drive their maintained, rhythmic pacemaking, and that this reliance makes them vulnerable to stressors thought to contribute to Parkinson disease progression. In mice, this reliance increased with age: juvenile neurons used pacemaking mechanisms common to neurons not affected in Parkinson disease, and these mechanisms remained latent in adulthood.

subject: Chan et al. (2007)
object: Chan et al. (2007) found that blocking Cav1.3 calcium channels in adult mouse substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons made them revert to the juvenile form of pacemaking. This 'rejuvenation' protected the neurons in both in vitro and in vivo mouse models of Parkinson disease, which the authors suggested points to a new strategy that could slow or stop disease progression.

subject: Outeiro et al. (2007)
object: Outeiro et al. (2007) identified a potent inhibitor of sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) and found that inhibiting SIRT2 rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity and changed inclusion morphology in a cellular model of Parkinson disease. Genetic inhibition of SIRT2 with small interfering RNA also rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity. The inhibitors protected against dopaminergic cell death both in vitro and in a Drosophila model of Parkinson disease. The authors suggested that the results point to a link between neurodegeneration and aging.

subject: Tan et al. (2007)
object: Tan et al. (2007) studied glucocerebrosidase (GBA) mutations and the risk of Parkinson disease in Chinese patients.

subject: Tan et al. (2007)
object: In a case-control study of 418 PD patients and 468 race-, sex- and age-matched controls, Tan et al. (2007) found no association between the CYP1A2 -163C>A polymorphism (rs762551) and PD (P = 0.08). This variant is associated with high CYP1A2 inducibility, which makes carriers fast caffeine metabolizers.

subject: CYP1A2 c.-163C>A
object: CYP1A2

subject: Tan et al. (2007)
object: Tan et al. (2007) found that caffeine intake was significantly and inversely associated with PD (P = 2.01 x 10(-5)). Compared with low drinkers, the odds ratio was 0.71 (95% CI 0.50-1.00) for moderate drinkers and 0.47 (95% CI 0.34-0.65) for high drinkers. Multivariate analysis showed no interaction between caffeine and CYP1A2 genotype (P = 0.956). The authors concluded that the protective association was similar in fast and slow metabolizers, which supports animal evidence that both caffeine and its metabolite paraxanthine are neuroprotective.

subject: Mata et al. (2008)
object: In a case-control study of 721 patients with PD, 57 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and 554 healthy controls from 4 movement disorder clinics in the Seattle, Washington, area, Mata et al. (2008) genotyped the 2 most common GBA mutations, N370S and L444P. Heterozygote frequency was significantly higher in PD patients (2.9%; P less than 0.001) and DLB patients (3.5%; P = 0.045) than in controls (0.4%). The authors suggested that GBA mutations exert a large effect on susceptibility to Lewy body disorders at the individual level but are associated with a modest (approximately 3%) population-attributable risk in individuals of European ancestry.

subject: Gan-Or et al. (2008)
object: Gan-Or et al. (2008) screened an Israeli Ashkenazi Jewish cohort of 420 PD patients, 333 elderly controls, and 3,805 young controls for 8 GBA mutations. Two of these mutations are associated with mild Gaucher disease (N370S, R496H) and six with severe Gaucher disease (84GG, IVS2+1, V394L, D409H, L444P, RecTL). GBA carrier frequency was 17.9% in PD patients, compared with 4.2% in elderly controls and 6.35% in young controls.

subject: Gan-Or et al. (2008)
object: Gan-Or et al. (2008) found that 29% of GBA carriers among PD patients carried a severe Gaucher disease mutation, compared with 7% of GBA carriers among young controls. Severe GBA mutations increased the risk of PD 13.6-fold and mild mutations 2.2-fold. Mean age at PD onset was 55.7 years with severe mutations and 57.9 years with mild mutations, compared with 60.7 years in patients without known GBA or LRRK2 mutations.

subject: Gan-Or et al. (2008)
object: Gan-Or et al. (2008) also genotyped the PD patients and elderly controls for LRRK2 G2019S. PD patients carrying LRRK2 G2019S had an earlier age at onset. More than one-third of the PD patients carried a mutation in GBA or LRRK2.

subject: Gutti et al. (2008)
object: Gutti et al. (2008) emphasized the need for appropriate genotyping strategies for glucocerebrosidase (GBA) mutations in cohorts with Parkinson disease.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2009)
object: Pankratz et al. (2009) performed a genomewide association study in familial Parkinson disease, genotyping 857 familial PD cases and 867 controls, mostly Caucasian and non-Hispanic, on the Illumina HumanCNV370Duo array. They used logistic models under additive and recessive modes adjusted for gender and age. No result met genomewide significance by Bonferroni correction. The strongest association was with SNPs in the GAK/DGKQ region on chromosome 4p (rs11248060; additive model p = 3.4 x 10(-6), OR = 1.69), and meta-analysis with a previous case-control GWAS (Fung et al.) improved this to p = 2.5 x 10(-7).

subject: Pankratz et al. (2009)
object: Pankratz et al. (2009) suggested that GAK was a promising candidate in the 4p region because a previous expression study had found it among 137 genes differentially expressed in PD, with a 1.56-fold change in substantia nigra pars compacta. SNPs in TMEM175, which lies between GAK and DGKQ, showed no suggestive association.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2009)
object: Pankratz et al. (2009) found consistent evidence of association between familial PD and the SNCA region on chromosome 4q (additive model p = 5.5 x 10(-5), OR = 1.35 for the rs356229 minor allele). The associated SNPs lay in intron 4 and the 3-prime region of SNCA. rs356229 showed modest linkage disequilibrium with rs356219, a SNP previously associated with SNCA mRNA levels.

subject: Pankratz et al. (2009)
object: Pankratz et al. (2009) found association with the C17orf69/MAPT region on chromosome 17 under a recessive model (rs1724425; p = 2.0 x 10(-5), OR = 0.56), which improved to p = 9.8 x 10(-6) on meta-analysis. Minor alleles tagging the protective H2 haplotype also featured in the additive meta-analysis. The authors concluded that the data supported the existing hypothesis that the complex genomic region around MAPT is related to PD risk.

subject: Gao et al. (2009)
object: Gao et al. (2009) examined natural hair color in early adulthood and PD risk among 38,641 men (Health Professionals Follow-up Study) and 93,661 women (Nurses' Health Study) in the US, documenting 539 PD cases over 16-22 years of follow-up. PD risk increased with decreasing darkness of hair color; after adjustment for age, smoking, ethnicity and other covariates, pooled relative risks were 1, 1.40, 1.61, and 1.93 (95% CI 1.08-3.43) for black, brown, blond, and red hair, respectively. The association was particularly strong for PD onset before age 70 years (RR for red vs black hair 3.83), but not significant for onset at 70 years or older.

subject: Gao et al. (2009)
object: In a case-control study nested within the HPFS and NHS cohorts (272 PD cases and 1,185 matched controls genotyped), Gao et al. (2009) found that homozygosity for the loss-of-function MC1R Arg151Cys polymorphism, which was strongly associated with red hair (RR 57), was associated with increased PD risk relative to Arg/Arg (adjusted RR 3.15; 95% CI 1.06-9.37); heterozygotes had RR 1.23. Participants with red hair who were Cys/Cys homozygotes had an RR of 4.9 compared with non-red-haired noncarriers. The authors suggested a potential role of pigmentation in PD, which may in part explain the co-occurrence of PD and melanoma.

object: MC1R

subject: Neumann et al. (2009)
object: Neumann et al. (2009) screened the GBA gene in 790 British patients with Parkinson disease and 257 controls matched for age and ethnicity. GBA mutations were found in 33 of 790 patients (4.18%) and 3 of 257 controls (1.17%), a significant difference (P = 0.01; odds ratio 3.7; 95% CI 1.12-12.14). Fourteen different GBA mutations were identified, including 3 previously undescribed ones, K7E, D443N, and G193E.

subject: Neumann et al. (2009)
object: Neumann et al. (2009) found that Parkinson disease patients carrying GBA mutations had early disease onset, hallucinations in 45% (14 of 31), and symptoms of cognitive decline or dementia in 48% (15 of 31).

subject: Neumann et al. (2009)
object: Neumann et al. (2009) found on neuropathologic examination widespread and abundant alpha-synuclein pathology in all 17 GBA mutation carriers studied, graded Braak stage 5-6, with McKeith limbic or diffuse neocortical Lewy body-type pathology. Diffuse neocortical Lewy body-type pathology tended to be more frequent in GBA mutation carriers than in matched Parkinson disease controls without GBA mutations.

subject: Neumann et al. (2009)
object: Neumann et al. (2009) concluded that GBA mutations were found in British Parkinson disease patients at a higher frequency than any other known Parkinson disease gene, and suggested that GBA mutations are a significant risk factor and, to date, the most common genetic factor identified for the disease.

subject: Gao et al. (2009)
object: Gao et al. (2009) conducted a genome-wide linkage screen of 5,824 SNPs in 278 families of European, non-Hispanic descent with Parkinson disease. Using parametric and nonparametric linkage analyses allowing for genetic heterogeneity, they found significant evidence for linkage on chromosome 18q11 (maximum lod score = 4.1) and suggestive evidence for linkage on chromosome 3q25 (maximum lod score = 2.5).

subject: Gao et al. (2009)
object: Gao et al. (2009) found that the linkage results on 18q11 and 3q25 were strongest in families not previously screened for linkage, and simulation studies suggested that these findings were likely due to locus heterogeneity rather than random statistical error.

subject: Gan-Or et al. (2009)
object: Gan-Or et al. (2009) reported a differential phenotype in Parkinson disease patients carrying severe versus mild GBA mutations.

subject: Lees et al. (2009)
object: In a review, Lees et al. (2009) described Parkinson disease as a common progressive bradykinetic disorder that can be accurately diagnosed. It is characterized by severe loss of nigral cells in the pars compacta and by accumulation of aggregated alpha-synuclein in specific brainstem, spinal cord and cortical regions. The authors stated that age is the main known risk factor.

subject: Lees et al. (2009)
object: Lees et al. (2009) noted that susceptibility genes, including alpha-synuclein, LRRK2 and GBA, have shown that genetic predisposition is another important causal factor in Parkinson disease.

subject: Lees et al. (2009)
object: Lees et al. (2009) stated that dopamine replacement therapy considerably reduces motor handicap in Parkinson disease. They added that effective treatment of associated depression, pain, constipation and nighttime problems can improve quality of life, and that embryonic stem cells and gene therapy are promising approaches still under research.

subject: Herrero Hernández (2009)
object: In a letter, Herrero Hernández (2009) discussed pigmentation as a possible clue to understanding the link between Parkinson disease and melanoma.

subject: Gao et al. (2009)
object: In a prospective study of 157,036 men and women in 2 US cohorts (the Health Professionals Follow-up Study and the Nurses' Health Study), Gao et al. (2009) identified 616 incident PD cases during 14 to 20 years of follow-up. A family history of melanoma in a first-degree relative was associated with a higher risk of PD (multivariate relative risk 1.85; 95% CI 1.2-2.8; p = 0.004) after adjustment for smoking, ethnicity, caffeine intake, and other covariates. A family history of colorectal, lung, prostate, or breast cancer was not significantly associated with PD risk. The authors concluded that melanoma and PD share common genetic components.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) pooled GBA genotype data from 16 centers on 4 continents, covering 5,691 patients with Parkinson disease (780 Ashkenazi Jews) and 4,898 controls (387 Ashkenazi Jews). Every center found more GBA mutations in patients than in controls. Across centers, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio for carrying any GBA mutation was 5.43 (95% CI 3.89-7.57) after excluding the Tokyo and Norway centers. The authors concluded that GBA mutations are likely a susceptibility factor rather than a Mendelian cause of PD, and are among the most common risk factors for PD identified to date.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that, when screening only for the GBA mutations N370S and L444P, one of the two was present in 15.3% of Ashkenazi Jewish PD patients versus 3.4% of Ashkenazi controls. In non-Ashkenazi subjects, the figures were 3.2% of patients versus 0.6% of controls. The combined Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio was 3.96 for N370S and 6.73 for L444P. N370S was especially common among Ashkenazi Jews (OR 5.62) and was not found in any Asian patient or control.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that about 20% (19.6%) of Ashkenazi Jewish PD patients carried a GBA mutation once 6 to 8 mutations were screened; 20% of the mutant alleles were neither L444P nor N370S, and the odds ratio was 6.48. In non-Ashkenazi subjects whose entire GBA coding region was sequenced, 6.9% of patients carried a mutation (OR 6.51). Among the 117 mutations identified, 54% were not N370S or L444P, so up to 46% of mutant alleles could be missed by screening only for those two. In addition, 22 of 43 subjects with L444P carried recombinant alleles that included pseudogene sequence.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that 17 PD patients, 15 of them Ashkenazi, carried two GBA mutations. Fourteen were homozygous for N370S, 2 were compound heterozygous for N370S and R496M, and 1 was compound heterozygous for N370S and V394L.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that the common GBA variants E326K and T369M, which are not pathogenic in Gaucher disease, were not significantly associated with Parkinson disease.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that PD patients with GBA mutations had an earlier mean age at onset than noncarriers (54.9 vs 58.8 years; p less than 0.001). Carriers were also more likely to report a first- or second-degree relative with PD (24.0% vs 17.8%). Carriers had significantly less asymmetric onset, bradykinesia, resting tremor and rigidity, and more cognitive changes (26.3% vs 19.0%). Orthostatic blood pressure changes and postural instability did not differ between the groups.

subject: Sidransky et al. (2009)
object: Sidransky et al. (2009) noted that two kinds of mechanism had been postulated for the link between GBA and PD. One is a gain of function through enhanced protein aggregation or lysosomal dysfunction; the other is a loss of function related to fluctuations in ceramide levels.

subject: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009)
object: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) performed a 2-stage genome-wide association study in individuals of European ancestry from the US, Germany, and Britain: 1,713 PD cases and 3,978 controls in stage I (463,185 SNPs), with replication in 3,361 cases and 4,573 controls. Two strong association signals were observed, at SNCA on chromosome 4q22 (rs2736990, OR = 1.23, combined P = 2.24 x 10(-16)) and at the MAPT locus on 17q21 (rs393152, OR = 0.77, P = 1.95 x 10(-16)). The authors concluded that the data demonstrated an unequivocal role for common genetic variants in the etiology of typical PD.

subject: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009)
object: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) found that 3 of the 4 significantly associated SNCA SNPs lay in the 3-prime LD block, suggesting that the causal variant is in the 3-prime region of SNCA, possibly affecting post-transcriptional RNA processing or stability. The REP1 microsatellite risk allele was in LD with the 3-prime risk alleles (r2 = 0.365 with rs3857059), and conditional analysis indicated the REP1 association was not independent. SNCA risk SNPs in PD differed from those associated with multiple system atrophy.
